remember: An idiom is a fixed phrase inside your own sentence; a proverb is a complete sentence with a moral.
Keep the frozen form: mit dem Bade, im Schilde, auf verlorenem Posten; conjugate only the verb.
The person is dative: jemandem den Rang ablaufen, jemandem das Wasser reichen, jemandem reinen Wein einschenken.
In commentary an idiom is a judgement — read what the writer thinks of the people it describes.

context.de: Die Regierung hat die Bahnreform jahrelang auf die lange Bank geschoben. Inzwischen ist das Land beim Schienenverkehr ins Hintertreffen geraten, und die Nachbarstaaten haben ihm längst den Rang abgelaufen. Wer nun jedoch die gesamte Bahn privatisieren will, schüttet das Kind mit dem Bade aus. Ein tragfähiges Konzept lässt sich nicht aus dem Ärmel schütteln — aber die Flinte ins Korn zu werfen, wäre die schlechteste aller Lösungen. Es ist Zeit, den Bürgern reinen Wein einzuschenken.
context.en: For years the government shelved the railway reform. Meanwhile the country has fallen behind in rail transport, and its neighbours outstripped it long ago. But anyone who now wants to privatise the entire railway is throwing the baby out with the bathwater. A viable plan cannot be conjured out of thin air — but throwing in the towel would be the worst of all solutions. It is time to tell citizens the plain truth.

mistakes.wrong: das Kind mit dem Badewasser ausschütten
mistakes.right: das Kind mit dem Bade ausschütten
mistakes.why: The idiom keeps the old dative form Bade; the English bathwater does not carry over.

mistakes.wrong: Er stand auf einem verlorenen Posten.
mistakes.right: Er stand auf verlorenem Posten.
mistakes.why: The idiom has no article, so the adjective takes the strong ending -em.

mistakes.wrong: Das Start-up hat den Marktführer den Rang abgelaufen.
mistakes.right: Das Start-up hat dem Marktführer den Rang abgelaufen.
mistakes.why: The person who is overtaken is in the dative; den Rang is the accusative object.

mistakes.wrong: Was führt er im Schild?
mistakes.right: Was führt er im Schilde?
mistakes.why: im Schilde is frozen with the old dative -e.

help.hook: Handle the Latin-flavoured words of serious German prose, like eruieren, obsolet and de facto, precisely and without false friends.
help.intro: Educated German (Bildungssprache) draws on a stock of Latin-derived words and phrases that rarely occur in everyday talk but run through every quality newspaper, court judgment and academic text: evident, eruieren, obsolet, prekär, konzedieren, implizieren, subsumieren, stringent, sukzessive, and set Latin phrases such as a priori, de facto, per se, ad hoc, Status quo and sui generis. The goal is to read them without hesitation and use them precisely in your own writing. In this quiz the German line above each sentence gives a plain paraphrase and the cue gives the English; type the Fremdwort, inflected to fit the sentence (prekären, konzediert, eruiert). Adjectives and verbs follow normal German grammar; the Latin phrases never inflect. Watch out for false friends with English: eventuell means possibly, not eventually, and konsequent means consistent, not consequent.

tips.title: German grammar on Latin stems
tips.text: Verbs in -ieren are regular and take no ge- in the Partizip II: eruieren → eruiert, konzedieren → konzediert, implizieren → impliziert, subsumieren → subsumiert. Adjectives take normal endings: unter prekären Bedingungen, eine stringente Argumentation, ein obsoletes Verfahren. Nouns keep their gender: das Desiderat, die Prämisse, der Status quo, das Diktum.

examples.de: Die Ursache des Ausfalls konnte bislang nicht eruiert werden.
examples.en: The cause of the outage has not yet been ascertained.

examples.de: Die Autorin konzediert, dass ihre Stichprobe klein ist.
examples.en: The author concedes that her sample is small.

tips.trap: geeruiert or gekonzediert do not exist: verbs in -ieren never take ge-.

check.q: Die Ursache wurde inzwischen ____. (identifizieren)
check.why: Verbs in -ieren never take ge- in the Partizip II: identifiziert, like eruiert and konzediert.

tips.title: Latin phrases stay invariable
tips.text: a priori (von vornherein), a posteriori (aus der Erfahrung, im Nachhinein), de facto (tatsächlich) vs de jure (rechtlich), per se (an sich), ad hoc (eigens, spontan), sui generis (eigener Art), Status quo (bestehender Zustand), ceteris paribus (unter sonst gleichen Bedingungen). They take no endings; only Status quo behaves like a noun with an article: den Status quo wahren.

examples.de: De jure ist der Präsident Oberbefehlshaber, de facto entscheidet das Parlament.
examples.en: In law the president is commander-in-chief; in practice parliament decides.

examples.de: Ob sich die Maßnahme bewährt, lässt sich erst a posteriori beurteilen.
examples.en: Whether the measure proves itself can only be judged in retrospect.

check.q: 'Legally she owns the firm, but in practice her brother runs it.' ____ ist sie die Eigentümerin.
check.why: de jure means by law, as opposed to de facto, in actual practice.

tips.title: Precision, not decoration
tips.text: Each Fremdwort says something the everyday word does not quite say. evident is stronger than klar; stringent describes the logic of an argument, not its strictness; marginal means negligible in extent; ambivalent means torn between two feelings, not indifferent; kontraproduktiv means working against one’s own goal. Use one where it sharpens the statement — a sentence stuffed with Latinisms reads as pompous.

examples.de: Die Unterschiede sind marginal und ändern nichts am Ergebnis.
examples.en: The differences are negligible and change nothing about the result.

examples.de: Ein Boykott wäre in dieser Phase kontraproduktiv.
examples.en: A boycott would be counter-productive at this stage.

tips.trap: ambivalent is not indifferent (gleichgültig): an ambivalent person feels two things at once.

check.q: Sie freut sich auf den Umzug und fürchtet ihn zugleich. Ihre Gefühle sind ____.
check.why: ambivalent means torn between two feelings at once, not indifferent (gleichgültig).

tips.title: Beware of English look-alikes
tips.text: Several Latinate words mean something different in German. eventuell = possibly (eventually = schließlich); konsequent = consistent, rigorous (consequent = folgend); sensibel = sensitive (sensible = vernünftig); prägnant = concise (pregnant = schwanger); rentabel = profitable. Check every look-alike before you use it in an essay.

examples.de: Die Regierung hat die Reform konsequent umgesetzt.
examples.en: The government implemented the reform consistently.

examples.de: Wir kommen eventuell etwas später.
examples.en: We may possibly come a bit later.

check.q: 'She reacts very sensitively to criticism': Sie reagiert sehr ____ auf Kritik.
check.why: German sensibel means sensitive; English 'sensible' is vernünftig, and prägnant means concise.

remember: Verbs in -ieren: no ge- in the Partizip II (eruiert, konzediert, impliziert).
Adjectives inflect normally (unter prekären Bedingungen); Latin phrases never do (a priori, de facto, per se, ad hoc).
Use a Fremdwort for precision, not decoration — one per sentence is usually enough.
False friends: eventuell = possibly, konsequent = consistent, sensibel = sensitive.

context.de: Dass die bisherige Förderpraxis obsolet ist, gilt in der Fachwelt als evident. Umstritten ist hingegen, wie sie zu ersetzen wäre. Die Kommission soll zunächst eruieren, welche Betriebe de facto profitieren; erst dann lässt sich die Prämisse prüfen, dass Subventionen per se Innovation fördern. Selbst die Befürworter konzedieren, dass eine stringente Evaluation bislang ein Desiderat geblieben ist. Die Umstellung soll daher sukzessive erfolgen und nicht ad hoc.
context.en: That the previous funding practice is obsolete is regarded among experts as self-evident. What is disputed, by contrast, is how it should be replaced. The commission is first to ascertain which businesses actually benefit; only then can the premise that subsidies promote innovation in themselves be tested. Even the supporters concede that a rigorous evaluation has so far remained a desideratum. The changeover is therefore to take place gradually and not at short notice.

mistakes.wrong: Die Zahl der Betroffenen wurde geeruiert.
mistakes.right: Die Zahl der Betroffenen wurde eruiert.
mistakes.why: Verbs in -ieren form the Partizip II without ge-.

mistakes.wrong: Nach langem Streit einigten sie sich eventuell.
mistakes.right: Nach langem Streit einigten sie sich schließlich.
mistakes.why: eventuell means possibly; for eventually German uses schließlich or letztendlich.

mistakes.wrong: unter prekär Bedingungen
mistakes.right: unter prekären Bedingungen
mistakes.why: A Latin-derived adjective before a noun takes the normal German ending.

mistakes.wrong: Die Bevölkerung ist dem Projekt gegenüber ambivalent, es ist ihr egal.
mistakes.right: Die Bevölkerung ist dem Projekt gegenüber gleichgültig.
mistakes.why: ambivalent means torn between opposing feelings, not indifferent.

title: Deutsch in Österreich und der Schweiz

help.hook: Read a Viennese menu or a Zurich notice without stumbling: Marillen, Jänner, Velo and Billett are standard German too.
help.intro: German is a pluricentric language: Germany, Austria and Switzerland each have their own standard variety, and Austrian and Swiss Standard German are no less correct than the German spoken in Hamburg — they are not dialects. They differ above all in vocabulary: Austria says Jänner, Paradeiser, Erdäpfel, Marillen, Topfen, Obers, Matura, Trafik and heuer; Switzerland says Velo, parkieren, grillieren, Trottoir, Billett, Znüni, Estrich (attic) and allenfalls (if necessary); both say Spital. There are also a few grammar differences, such as the perfect with sein (ich bin gesessen), and Swiss spelling never uses ß. The goal is to read Austrian and Swiss newspapers, official letters and recipes without stumbling. In this quiz the German line tells you the region and the word used in Germany; type the Austrian or Swiss standard word — or, in the two items marked with an arrow, the German-German equivalent.

tips.title: Austria: the kitchen and the calendar
tips.text: Jänner (Januar), Paradeiser (Tomaten), Erdäpfel (Kartoffeln), Marillen (Aprikosen), Topfen (Quark), Obers / Schlagobers (Sahne), Karfiol (Blumenkohl), Kren (Meerrettich), Sessel (Stuhl), Matura (Abitur), Trafik (Tabak- und Zeitschriftenladen), heuer (dieses Jahr). When Austria joined the EU in 1995, a protocol gave 23 Austrian food terms — among them Erdäpfel, Marillen, Topfen, Paradeiser and Obers — equal legal standing with their German-German counterparts.

examples.de: Heuer gibt es besonders viele Marillen.
examples.en: This year there are particularly many apricots.

examples.de: Die Matura findet im Mai statt.
examples.en: The school-leaving exam takes place in May.

tips.trap: Sessel in Austria is an ordinary chair; the upholstered armchair is a Fauteuil.

check.q: ‘apricot’ in Austrian standard German:
check.why: Marille is the Austrian apricot; Paradeiser is a tomato and Topfen is quark.

tips.title: Switzerland: French loans and -ieren
tips.text: Swiss Standard German borrows from French and likes the ending -ieren: Velo (Fahrrad), Trottoir (Gehweg), Billett (Fahrkarte), Poulet (Hähnchen), Glace (Eis), parkieren (parken), grillieren (grillen). Everyday life has its own words: Znüni (mid-morning snack), Estrich (Dachboden), Gesuch (Antrag), Busse (Geldstrafe), allenfalls (gegebenenfalls), Matur or Matura (Abitur). Spital (Krankenhaus) is standard in both Switzerland and Austria.

examples.de: Das Velo darf nicht auf dem Trottoir parkiert werden.
examples.en: The bike may not be parked on the pavement.

examples.de: Allfällige Fragen beantworten wir gern; allenfalls rufen wir Sie zurück.
examples.en: We are happy to answer any questions; if necessary we will call you back.

tips.trap: Estrich in Germany is floor screed; in Switzerland it is the attic. allenfalls in Germany means at most, in Switzerland if necessary.

check.q: In Zürich: Ich fahre jeden Tag mit dem ____ zur Arbeit. (= bicycle)
check.why: Velo is the Swiss standard word for bicycle; Billett is a ticket and Trottoir the pavement.

tips.title: Grammar and spelling
tips.text: In Austria, Switzerland and southern Germany sitzen, stehen and liegen form the perfect with sein: Ich bin gesessen, Das Auto ist vor dem Haus gestanden, Er ist im Bett gelegen. Swiss Standard German writes ss wherever Germany and Austria write ß: Strasse, Grüsse, schliesslich, gross. Some genders differ too: in Austria das Cola and das E-Mail are common, and in Switzerland das Tram.

examples.de: Wir sind lange vor dem Eingang gestanden.
examples.en: We stood in front of the entrance for a long time.

examples.de: Mit freundlichen Grüssen aus der Gemeindeverwaltung
examples.en: With kind regards from the municipal administration

check.q: How does a Swiss newspaper spell ‘street’?
check.why: Swiss Standard German never uses ß and writes ss instead.

tips.title: Standard, not dialect
tips.text: Everything in this quiz is written standard language: it appears in newspapers, laws, school books and official letters in Austria or Switzerland. Dialect is something else — Swiss German dialects (Schweizerdeutsch) and Austrian dialects are spoken varieties you are not expected to write. So Velo and Jänner belong in a formal written text; dialect spellings do not.

examples.de: Der Nationalrat tritt im Jänner wieder zusammen.
examples.en: The National Council reconvenes in January.

examples.de: Das Billett gilt nur für die zweite Klasse.
examples.en: The ticket is only valid for second class.

check.q: Which line is Swiss Standard German, fit for an official notice?
options: Bitte lösen Sie vor der Fahrt ein Billett.
Bitte lösed Sie vor de Fahrt es Billett.
check.answer: Bitte lösen Sie vor der Fahrt ein Billett.
check.why: Billett is written standard in Switzerland; the dialect forms lösed, de and es belong to spoken Swiss German, not to formal writing.

context.de: Heuer ist die Wienerin Anna nach der Matura für ein Praktikum nach Zürich gezogen. Anfangs ist sie oft ratlos vor dem Fahrplan gestanden: Statt einer Fahrkarte löst man dort ein Billett, zur Arbeit fährt man mit dem Velo, und wer falsch parkiert, zahlt eine Busse. Im Büro gibt es um zehn das Znüni, und ihre Wohnung hat einen Estrich, wo sie die Koffer verstaut. Nur beim Einkaufen vermisst sie ihre Marillen und den Topfen — in Zürich heißen sie Aprikosen und Quark.
context.en: This year, after her school-leaving exam, Anna from Vienna moved to Zurich for an internship. At first she often stood baffled in front of the timetable: instead of a Fahrkarte you buy a Billett there, you ride your Velo to work, and anyone who parks wrongly pays a fine. At the office there is the Znüni at ten, and her flat has an attic where she stores her suitcases. Only when shopping does she miss her Marillen and her Topfen — in Zurich they are called apricots and quark.

mistakes.wrong: Schweizerdeutsch und Schweizer Hochdeutsch sind dasselbe.
mistakes.right: Schweizerdeutsch ist Dialekt; Schweizer Hochdeutsch ist die geschriebene Standardsprache.
mistakes.why: Words like Velo and Billett belong to the written standard, not to dialect.

mistakes.wrong: Wir haben die Koffer in den Estrich gebracht. (in Germany, meaning the attic)
mistakes.right: Wir haben die Koffer auf den Dachboden gebracht.
mistakes.why: In Germany Estrich is floor screed; only in Switzerland is it the attic.

mistakes.wrong: Ich habe gesessen ist in Österreich falsch.
mistakes.right: In Österreich ist ich bin gesessen üblich; ich habe gesessen wird aber verstanden.
mistakes.why: The perfect with sein for sitzen/stehen/liegen is a regional standard feature, not an error either way.

help.hook: Gather the precise words of philosophy, science, law and literature, each with its article and its register.
help.intro: Every word this module’s exercises use, on one deck of flashcards: 365 cards, 184 of them nouns. The vocabulary of this module is precise, stylistically marked vocabulary: register pairs, legal and philosophical terms, and fixed expressions, from the themes Philosophie & Gesellschaft, Wissenschaftssprache, Recht & Verwaltung: Amtsdeutsch, Literatur: Lyrik & Deutung. Write the German, choose it from four options, or flip the card and rate yourself. A word you miss comes back later in the same run, and stays in your weak words until you get it right three times in a row.

tips.title: Register is part of the meaning
tips.text: Two words can mean the same and still not be interchangeable. The note on the back often names the plain or colloquial equivalent; learn which one fits a formal text.

tips.title: Three modes, three kinds of memory
tips.text: Choose trains recognition, Write trains recall, and Flip trains honesty with yourself. Start a new deck in Choose, move to Write once most cards feel familiar, and use Flip for a fast review before you need the words — a meeting, a letter, a trip.

examples.en: power of judgement

examples.de: die Unmündigkeit

check.why: Compounds take the gender of their last part: die Kraft, so die Urteilskraft.

tips.title: A noun without its article is marked wrong
tips.text: In Write mode a noun only counts with der, die or das in front of it. The card tells you when you had the right word but left the article off, so you know exactly what to fix.

examples.en: categorical imperative

examples.de: der freie Wille
examples.en: free will (den freien Willen, des freien Willens)

check.q: Er bestreitet ____. (free will)
check.why: bestreiten takes the accusative: der freie Wille becomes den freien Willen, with -en on both adjective and noun.

remember: Never say a noun without its article, not even in your head.
Miss a word? It comes back in the same run. Three correct answers in a row take it off the weak list.
Verbs and adjectives have no article: type them as they stand, like "selbst".

help.hook: A crowded antique shop full of rare old things: find each one in the picture, then give it its article.
help.intro: A picture hunt instead of a deck: one crowded antique shop with 32 old things to find in it, every one a precise noun you rarely need until you walk into a place like this — der Sekretär, das Spinnrad, die Balkenwaage, das Butterfass, der Paravent. The prompt asks Wo ist die Registrierkasse? The prompt asks for one object, and you tap it in the picture. Each find shows its label, coloured by its gender, then leaves a small tick in that colour, so you can see what you have already found. A tap on the wrong object tells you what you hit and you keep looking; after three misses the right one is shown. Once you have passed a run, the hunt turns harder: the prompt hides the article (Wo ist ___ Brille?), and after the find you choose der, die or das yourself. No object is asked twice in the same run.

tips.title: A compound takes the gender of its last part
tips.text: Most of the shop is compounds, and the last part decides the article, however unusual the first part is. Butter + Fass: das Fass, so das Butterfass. Kaffee + Mühle: die Mühle, so die Kaffeemühle. Schirm + Ständer: der Ständer, so der Schirmständer.

examples.de: die Balkenwaage
examples.en: balance scale (die Waage)

examples.de: das Schaukelpferd, Plural: -e
examples.en: rocking horse (das Pferd)

check.q: ____ Ohrensessel steht vor dem Paravent.
check.why: The last part is der Sessel, so the whole word is der Ohrensessel.

tips.title: Same thing, different word, different gender
tips.text: Two clocks, two different last parts: die Standuhr and die Sanduhr both end in die Uhr, but das Pendel inside the clock is neuter. And a desk is der Tisch, yet the bureau is der Sekretär, while the counter is die Ladentheke. Learn each word with its own article, never by the meaning.

examples.de: die Sanduhr
examples.en: hourglass (die Uhr)

examples.de: das Pendel
examples.en: pendulum

check.q: Which article goes with Pendel?
check.why: Pendel is neuter: das Pendel, plural die Pendel.

tips.title: Loanwords keep a gender of their own
tips.text: Many antique-shop words came from French or Greek: der Sekretär, der Paravent, das Grammophon, das Akkordeon, der Globus. Say them aloud with the article as one unit — der Paravent, das Grammophon — and the colour on the label (blue der, red die, green das) gives your eye a second hook.

Loanwords have their own gender: der Sekretär, der Paravent, das Grammophon, das Akkordeon.
Der Globus has an unusual plural: die Globen.

help.hook: An old fishing harbour full of nautical gear: find each thing on the quay or the water, then give it its article.

A tap on the wrong object tells you what you hit and you keep looking; after three misses the right one is shown. Once you have passed a run, the hunt turns harder: the prompt hides the article (Wo ist ___ Brille?), and after the find you choose der, die or das yourself. tips.title: A compound takes the gender of its last part
tips.text: Harbour words are almost all compounds. Schiff + Glocke: die Glocke, so die Schiffsglocke. Steuer + Haus: das Haus, so das Steuerhaus. Hummer + Korb: der Korb, so der Hummerkorb. Find the last word and you have the article.
